alex.k: Quick q — trying to capture short nsys traces for runtime perf debugging (kernel selection, batching heuristics, KV-cache behavior). What minimal nsys flags do people use so files stay manageable but NVTX and CUDA kernels show up?

priya: For our batched runs I usually do a 20–30s sample window and trace cuda+nvtx+osrt. Example CLI we run from CI: 

```
nsys profile \
  --output=profiles/1750001234_redwood \
  --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --sample=cpu \
  --duration=30s \
  --force-overwrite \
  -- python -u tools/run_inference.py --config bench/bert_batch.yaml
```

priya: Notes: `--sample=cpu` keeps the capture size down. If you need every API call and exact kernel timing, remove `--sample` (full tracing) but expect 5–10x larger files.

jhansen: +1. Also: annotate the hot sections with NVTX so you can capture exact batch boundaries/KV ops. Example in Python: 

```
import torch
torch.cuda.nvtx.range_push("batch:step1")
# read from kv cache or run kernel
torch.cuda.nvtx.range_pop()
```

jhansen: Then in Nsight UI filter by NVTX names to correlate kernels with KV hits/misses.

maya: If you suspect a specific kernel regression, do a short full-trace for that exact iteration: set `--duration=5s` and wrap the exact workload with NVTX ranges so you only capture the noisy part. Also set `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` if you want single-GPU timeline.

simeon: One more trick — use `--capture-range=nvtx:my_trace_start,my_trace_end` to let nsys only record between NVTX push/pop pairs (less overhead than full process trace). Example: start your run with `nvtx.range_push("profile:start")` and finish with `nvtx.range_push("profile:end")`.

alex.k: Do we have a recommended naming/rotation scheme for traces? Trying to avoid filling the CI disk.

priya: We put them in s3 after a quick `nsys stats` pass and only keep traces > 10MB locally. Our script: 

```
nsys profile --output=/tmp/profile_$TS --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --duration=20s -- python ...
nsys stats /tmp/profile_$TS.qdrep || true   # quick sanity check
if [ $(stat -c%s /tmp/profile_$TS.qdrep) -gt 10485760 ]; then
  aws s3 cp /tmp/profile_$TS.qdrep s3://redwood-traces/$TS.qdrep
fi
rm /tmp/profile_$TS.*
```

maya: When you open in `nsys-ui` look at the CUDA Kernel lane and the API/Driver lanes. Long gaps with small memcpy/kern launches often indicate KV cache misses or stall on IO. Also use the timeline search for `memcpy` and `cudaLaunchKernel`.

simeon: For perf regressions, export an aggregated report and diff them: `nsys stats --report=summary profile1.qdrep` and compare kernel durations and launch counts. That surfaces FPS drops very quickly.

alex.k: Awesome, thanks. One last : do we capture osrt always? What's osrt buying us?

priya: osrt captures OS thread scheduling/events which helps if you suspect CPU-side batching delays or thread preemption. We enable it by default for CI captures; disable only when you need smallest possible files.
